title: Bi-Criteria Metric Distortion
one_liner: Ask what happens when a voting rule may choose a small committee instead of one winner, and measure how much that extra freedom reduces the cost created by using only rankings.
lead: Metric distortion studies what is lost when voters provide only rankings instead of exact utility numbers. In that framework, voters and candidates are points in a metric space, and the social cost depends on distance. Most prior work asked for one winner. This paper asks a broader question: if a rule may choose a committee of k candidates and each voter is served by the closest committee member, can the committee achieve lower distortion than any single winner? The answer depends sharply on the shape of the space. On a line, a constant-size committee can match the optimum cost. In two-dimensional spaces and on trees, that hope collapses unless the committee contains all candidates. The result matters because it separates the power of committee choice from the constraints imposed by the underlying space.

problem.h2: Why one-winner distortion leaves an open committee question
paras: In metric distortion, rankings are easier for voters to report than exact utilities, but rankings hide intensity. Distortion measures how much extra social cost can result from that loss of information.

For one winner, the existing theory is well studied. The new question is whether allowing a committee of several candidates changes the picture when each voter is matched to the nearest chosen candidate. This is important because committee choice introduces a second resource: the rule may spend more winners to reduce service distance. The paper asks whether that extra resource can systematically overcome the information loss from ordinal rankings.

callout.html: Measure distortion with two resources at once, chosen committee size and service cost, because committee freedom may or may not offset the information lost in rankings.

paras: The paper changes metric distortion from a one-winner question into a bi-criteria question that trades committee size against service cost.
object.object: the resource counted in the distortion analysis

hidden.name: coverage power of a small committee under a given space shape
paras: The hidden quantity is how much of the metric space a small committee can cover without exact distance information. A committee helps only if a few representatives can stand close enough to many voters at once, because each voter is served by the nearest chosen member.

That quantity depends on the shape of the space. On a line, a few well-placed representatives can cover intervals efficiently. In two-dimensional spaces or on trees, local branching creates many directions to cover, so a small committee can miss some groups badly. This is why the paper gets a sharp separation across metrics.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark settings where a small committee can cover voters well despite the loss of cardinal information.

reads.html: The real issue is whether a few winners can stand close enough to everyone once the shape of the space is taken into account.
Bi-criteria distortion depends on coverage power because committee size can reduce cost only when the metric lets a few chosen candidates serve many voters well.

mechanism.h2: Why the shape of the space changes everything
paras: A committee reduces service cost by letting each voter attach to the nearest chosen candidate. That creates a covering problem: can a few chosen points stand near all voters?

On a line, the answer is often yes. Order structure is simple, and a few committee members can partition the line into intervals with controlled distance. This is why the paper can obtain optimal cost with only a constant number of selected candidates in that setting.

In two-dimensional spaces and on trees, the situation changes. Branching and multiple directions create coverage demands that a small committee cannot satisfy uniformly. Even if rankings reveal relative order, they do not reveal enough metric detail to place a tiny committee optimally across all branches. That is why the lower bounds become strong: unless one selects essentially everyone, some voter groups remain costly.

math.words: For a chosen committee, voter cost is distance to the nearest committee member. Distortion compares the total or worst voter cost of the ranking-based committee against the best committee with full metric knowledge.
symbols: the committee chosen using only ordinal rankings
the best committee of the allowed size when exact distances are known
either the sum of voter distances or the maximum voter distance
how much extra cost is paid because only rankings are used

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose three neighborhoods lie on a line and the rule may choose two representatives.
If the ranking-based rule chooses two candidates that sit near the outer neighborhoods, the total voter distance may be 10.
Assume the exact-distance optimum with two representatives also has total distance 10.
Then distortion is 10 / 10 = 1, which is perfect.
If the same style of choice in a branching tree leaves one branch uncovered and raises total distance to 18 while the exact-distance optimum is 10, distortion becomes 1.8.

math.note: The paper studies both sum cost and worst-case cost, but the central comparison is always ranking-based committee cost against metric-optimal committee cost.

items.b: Committee size alone does not guarantee low distortion.
items.html: Adding a few winners may still fail badly in complex space shapes because the missing metric information leaves the rule unable to place them where coverage is needed most.

items.b: A result for one metric may not transfer.
items.html: Line-based intuition can break in trees or in the plane, because branching and directional spread create obstacles that do not exist on a line.
A committee that looks good under total distance may still leave one group far away, because utilitarian and egalitarian goals weigh coverage differently.
The bi-criteria view is useful because it reveals exactly when extra winners can offset ordinal information loss and when the space shape prevents that rescue.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create three synthetic electorates: one on a line, one on a two-dimensional plane, and one on a tree. Let voters report only rankings over candidates. Compare the best ranking-based committee of size k with the best committee that knows exact distances.

The demo should plot distortion as k grows under both total-distance and worst-distance objectives. A convincing result shows quick approach to distortion 1 on the line and much slower or impossible approach in the plane and on trees because the space shape controls how useful extra committee seats really are.
demo.closing: The key lesson is that more winners help only when the metric lets a few candidates cover the space well, because otherwise some voter groups remain far from every chosen representative.
